CODE OF PRACTICE FOR SELECTION, INSTALLATION, OPERATION AND MAINTENANCE OF PUMPS FOR INDUSTRIAL APPLICATIONS
PART 4 MAINTENANCE

. Scope -

Lays down general guidelines for maintenance of pumps for industrial applications.

.l This standard is not applicable to pumps for agricultural applications. I. Maintena'nce - A pump can not give smooth service in the absence of proper maintenance. lence due attention should be paid to the maintenance of the pumps in operation as well as auxiliary lumps. 1.1 Daily Observation of Pump Operations -For continuous duty pumps, hourly and daily nspection should be made. Whenever any irregularities in the operation of a pump are observed, nmediate report of the same, should be made. This particularly applies to changes in the sound of running pump, abrupt changes in bearing temperatures and stuffing box leakage. Recording nstruments, if provided, should be checked every day to determine whether the capacity, pressure or lower consumption indicate that further inspection is required. Pressure gauges and flowmeters, if Depending upon the criticality and application paranstalled, should be checked very frequently. neters, such as ahead, power, bearing temperature and sump level vibration, should be monitered. The nonitoring criteria differs from application to application. !.2 Annual Inspection 2.2.1 Centrifugal pumps :arried out. When general overhauls are carried out the following checks shall bE

2.2.1 .l Radial clearance between impeller and wearing ring, wear of the part of the shaft or sleeve )n which the stuffing box is mounted, examination of ah parts for corrosion, abrasion or pitting whict :an cause losses if on the fixed parts and serious unbalancing if on the moving parts, alignment, ant :hecks on the coupling, replacing of the packing or worn out parts of mechanical seal, check of bott adial and axial clearance of the bearings. 2.2.1.2 In case of gland packings it should never be tighted to the full extent with the pump a ;tand still, but the tightening should be regulated gradually and gently with the pump in motion so tha :he packing can dilate and settle and tightening should be stopped as soon as the leak ceases. 2.2.2 Reciprocating pumps ( crank end )

2.2.2.1 Crank endOverhaul envolving almost complete dismantling of the pump is carried ou oy speciafisedtechnician at comparatively long intervals and only when inevitable and consist of :
a) `checking

~of clearances and the condition of the surface main and big end bearings crosshead sliding block and guides and a complete renovation of normal clearances and conditions b insertion of antifriction metal grinding and scraping or by replacement. When renovating th bearings the instruction of the manufacturer should be observed scrupulously as regard th composition of anti-friction metal and the condition of melting; bolts, keys, coupling bolts, etc; and and repeated washing of.. o

b) a check of the foundation

c) complete overhauling of the lubricating pump and accessories circuit including crank case, holes, tubing, etc.

2.2.2.2 Fluid end - Overhaul of the items in contact with the fluid, such as valves, stuffing bo) pistons mhd cylinders is carried out at more frequent intervals apart from general overhauls. a) Valve seat group should be considered as one indivisible combination and not interchanceabl and should be ground as such. As to the stuffing boxes the instructions which ensure correct assembly and effective maintenance as supplied by the pump manufacturer shall hav to be rigorously observed.

b) Pistons - Only slight scoring or radial wear on the active part up to 0'2 mm allowable. In other cases remetalling and grinding is indispensible, with accurate machining. This is possible in case of stainless steel plungers. c) In case of chromium plated plungers small longitudinal scorings which do not remove chromium plated bright areas are acceptable but deep scoring, any discontinuity or flakingoff of the chromium plating requires extensive repairs. Plungers/pistons which are not plated and can not be welded require replacement when damaged. 2.3 All instruments and flow-metering devices should be recalibrated, and the pump should be tested to determine whether proper performance is being obtained. If internal repaiis are made, the pump should again be tested after completion of the repairs. 2.4 In order to ensure satisfactory operation of these pumps, the following checks are recommended depending upon the application : Weekly Monthly Quarterly Half-yearly Inspection and cleaning of strainers; Inspection of glands and stuffing boxes; Inspection of impellers, sealing rings and casing; and Inspection of bearings and.renewal Change of strainers, if required. of lubricants. additional maintenance

2.5 Spare and Repair Parts - The minimum number of spare parts which should be carried in stock In the absence shall be determined, to a great extent, on the basis of severity of service conditions. of prior experience, the pump manufacturer should be consulted on this subject. As on insurance against delays, spare parts should be ordered for the complete unit. Depending upon the requirements, certain replacement parts may have to be supplied either oversized or undersizes. When ordering spare parts after a pump has been in service, the manufacturer should always be This information is essential in given the pump serial number and size as stamped on the nameplate. identifying the pump exactly and in furnishing repair parts of correct size and material. 3. Inspection and Repair History Card - Details of all inspections and repairs should be entered on individual pump maintenance cards, which contain a complete record of ah the items requiring special These cards should al.50 co&in space for comments and observations on the condition of attention. the parts to be repaired or replaced, on the rate and appearance of wear, -and the rapair methods In many cases it is worthwhile to take photographs of badly worn parts before they followed. are repaired. In all cases complete record of the cost of maintenance and repairs should be kept for each individual pump, together with a record of hits operating hours. A study of these records will generally~reveal whether a change in materials or even a minor change in construction may be the most econominal course of action. 4. Diagnosis of Pump Troubles and Remedies - Pump operating troubles may be either of a hydraulic or of a mechanical nature. In the first categary. a pump may fail to deliver liquid, it may deliver an insufficient volume rate of flow or develop insufficient pressure, or it may consume excessive power, or symptoms of mechanical troubles may develop at the stuffing boxes or at the bearings, or vibration, noise or breakage of some pump parts may occur. There is a definite interdependence between some difficulties of both categories. For example, increased wear at the running clearances must be classified as a mechanical trouble, but it will result in a reduction of the net pump volume rate of flow - a hydraulic symptom - without necessarily causing a mechanical breakdown or even excessive vibration. A diagnostic analysis along with-remedies is presented in Tables 1 to 3.
